answers.brief_reasoning: Loop rule: ε − IR − q/C = 0, with I = dq/dt. So dq/dt = (εC − q)/(RC). Separate variables: dq/(εC − q) = dt/(RC). Integrate from q = 0 at t = 0: −ln((εC − q)/(εC)) = t/(RC).
Time constant RC = (5000 Ω)(50×10⁻⁶ F) = 0.25 s, so t = 250 ms is exactly one time constant. Final charge εC = (6 V)(50 µF) = 300 µC. Then q = 300 µC × (1 − e⁻¹) = 300 × 0.632 ≈ 190 µC.

The final charge is Q = εC. When charging is complete the current is zero, so there is no voltage across the resistor and R does not affect Q. Half charge is reached when 1 − e^(−t/RC) = 1/2, giving t½ = RC ln2. This time is proportional to R, so doubling R doubles it.
answers.final_answer: The final charge does not change (it stays 300 µC). The time to reach half the final charge doubles (factor of 2).
